full.text: Gregor Mendel studied inheritance in garden peas and found that characters are controlled by inherited factors, now called genes.
One of two or more alternative forms of a gene found at the same locus on homologous chromosomes.
The alleles an organism has, for example Tt.
The observable characteristic, resulting from the genotype and the environment.

items: Law of segregation: the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation, so each gamete carries one allele
Law of independent assortment: alleles of different genes on different chromosomes assort independently

full.text: A dominant allele is expressed in the heterozygote; a recessive allele is expressed only when homozygous.

full.title: Past-paper tip
full.text: Always show the parental genotypes, the gametes and a Punnett square, then state the phenotypic ratio.

items: Gene: unit of inheritance; allele: alternative form

full.text: Neither allele is fully dominant, so the heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype.
Example: in snapdragons, red (RR) x white (WW) gives pink (RW). The F2 ratio is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.
Both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote.
Example: in the ABO blood groups, alleles IA and IB are codominant, so a person with IAIB has blood group AB. Roan coat colour in cattle is another example.

full.title: Past-paper tip
full.text: In both cases the phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio, 1:2:1, because each genotype has its own phenotype.

items: Codominance: both expressed (blood group AB, roan cattle)

full.text: In humans females are XX and males are XY. Genes carried on the X chromosome but not on the Y are sex-linked.
Males have only one X, so a single recessive X-linked allele is expressed. Females need two copies, so heterozygous females are carriers.

items: Examples: red-green colour blindness and haemophilia
A carrier mother (XHXh) and a normal father (XHY): half of the sons are expected to be affected
An affected father passes the allele to all his daughters but none of his sons

full.text: A heterozygous individual who has a recessive allele but does not show the condition.

full.title: Past-paper tip
full.text: Write sex-linked genotypes with the allele as a superscript on the X, for example XhY.

items: Males XY: one recessive allele is expressed
Father to son transmission does not occur

written.stem: State Mendel's law of segregation and explain it using a monohybrid cross.
written.model_answer: The two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation so each gamete has one allele. Tt x Tt gives gametes T and t from each parent; the offspring are 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, a 3 tall : 1 dwarf phenotypic ratio.

points.text: Correct cross / Punnett square Tt x Tt

written.stem: Distinguish between incomplete dominance and codominance with an example of each.
written.model_answer: In incomplete dominance the heterozygote is intermediate, for example pink snapdragons from red and white. In codominance both alleles are fully expressed, for example blood group AB (IAIB).

written.stem: Explain why haemophilia is more common in males than in females.
written.model_answer: Haemophilia is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. Males have one X and a Y, which has no matching allele, so one recessive allele causes the condition. Females need two recessive alleles; with one they are carriers.

points.text: Males have only one X / Y has no allele
Females need two alleles; heterozygotes are carriers

written.stem: What is a test cross? Explain how it shows the genotype of a tall pea plant.
written.model_answer: A test cross crosses an individual showing the dominant phenotype with a homozygous recessive individual. If all offspring are tall the plant is TT; if half are tall and half dwarf the plant is Tt.

written.stem: Explain a dihybrid cross in peas and how it supports the law of independent assortment.
written.model_answer: Round yellow (RRYY) is crossed with wrinkled green (rryy); the F1 are all RrYy round yellow. The F1 produce four kinds of gametes, RY, Ry, rY and ry, in equal numbers because the two genes assort independently. Selfing gives a 16-square Punnett square and an F2 ratio of 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green. New combinations appear, showing that alleles of different genes assort independently.

points.text: Four gamete types in equal numbers

written.stem: Describe how chromosomal mutations arise and give examples of their effects in humans.
written.model_answer: Changes in chromosome structure include deletion, duplication, inversion and translocation, often from errors in crossing over. Changes in number arise by non-disjunction, when chromosomes fail to separate in meiosis, giving gametes with an extra or missing chromosome. Examples are Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Turner syndrome (45, X) and Klinefelter syndrome (47, XXY).

points.text: Structural changes: deletion, duplication, inversion, translocation

ask.question: What is the difference between genotype and phenotype?
ask.answer: The genotype is the set of alleles an organism has for a character, for example Tt. The phenotype is the observable characteristic, for example tall, which results from the genotype and the environment.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 6.1: Mendelian inheritance

ask.question: What is the F2 ratio of a dihybrid cross?
ask.answer: For two unlinked genes with complete dominance, crossing two double heterozygotes (AaBb x AaBb) gives an F2 phenotypic ratio of 9:3:3:1.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 6.2: Monohybrid & dihybrid crosses

ask.question: What is codominance?
ask.answer: In codominance both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote. For example, a person with alleles IA and IB has blood group AB.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 6.4: Incomplete dominance & codominance

ask.question: Why is colour blindness more common in boys?
ask.answer: Red-green colour blindness is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. Boys have only one X, so one recessive allele is enough. Girls need two, and heterozygous girls are carriers.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 6.6: Sex linkage

ask.question: What is a test cross used for?
ask.answer: A test cross finds the genotype of an individual with a dominant phenotype. It is crossed with a homozygous recessive. All dominant offspring means it is homozygous; a 1:1 ratio means it is heterozygous.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 6.3: Test cross & back cross
